**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 58-year-old married man of African descent, a hairdresser by trade for over thirty years, who presents with a pervasive sense of dread he cannot shake. He describes the event that changed everything as occurring eight months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late autumn.

He had just closed his small salon, a place he built from nothing in a modest strip mall. The night was cold and damp. As he walked to his car, keys in hand, a young man emerged from the shadows between two parked vans. Mr. A. remembers the glint of a knife, the low, flat voice demanding his wallet and phone. He complied instantly, his hands trembling as he handed over his belongings. The man then shoved him hard against the driver’s side door. Mr. A. felt the cold metal of the knife blade press against his neck, just below his jaw. He remembers the smell of stale cigarettes and sweat, the sound of his own ragged breathing, and the terrifying, absolute certainty that he was about to die. Then, as quickly as it began, the man was gone, running into the dark, leaving Mr. A. slumped against his car, his heart hammering against his ribs.

Since that night, Mr. A. has not been the same man. He stopped driving to work. The drive, the exact same route he took that night, became impossible. The sight of the strip mall’s sign from a distance would send a jolt of panic through his chest, his palms slicking with sweat. Now, his wife, a kind woman who works in a hospital cafeteria, drives him. He sits in the passenger seat, his body rigid, scanning every pedestrian, every alleyway, every shadow. He cannot look out the side window; he only stares straight ahead.

At the salon, his hands, once steady and precise, now tremble. He has always taken pride in his work, in the quiet intimacy of cutting hair, the gentle conversation. Now, he flinches if a client touches his arm unexpectedly. The sound of a hair dryer’s cord scraping against the floor can make him drop his scissors. He has started positioning his chair so his back is always against the wall, his eyes fixed on the front door. He has also started locking the salon’s front door during his last appointment, a full hour before closing time, a practice his long-time clients have begun to notice. He tells them it’s for safety, a new policy.

The worst time is at night. He cannot sleep. His wife says he thrashes and cries out in his sleep, sometimes yelling “No, no, no!” in a voice she does not recognize. He has vivid, recurring nightmares: the knife, the smell of cigarettes, the freezing pressure on his throat. He wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart racing, convinced for a terrifying moment that the man is in the room with him. He has taken to sleeping on the couch in the living room, a baseball bat propped against the armrest. He tells his wife it’s for his back, but they both know it is a lie.

He has become irritable, short-tempered with his wife over small things—a misplaced remote, a slightly undercooked dinner. He feels a constant, low-level hum of anger and a profound sense of being cut off from his old life. He no longer attends the weekly community gatherings at his church, a place he once loved. He cannot bear the crowds, the bustle, the feeling of being exposed. He feels empty, numb, as if the man who was robbed that night is a stranger, and he is just a shell left behind. He came to therapy only after his wife pleaded with him, saying she felt she was losing him. He does not know if talking can help, but he knows he cannot keep living this way, trapped in a single, violent moment that refuses to end.
